en: No. 1672ka Title: Śivasūtravṛttiḥ Extent: 13 folios
Subject: Śaivadarśana, page 1a) Om, salutations to Śiva, the venerable Guru who possesses true knowledge. Om. Śrī.
Salutations to Śiva, the Guru who holds true knowledge. Om. Salutations.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ, salutations to Śiva.
Oṃ, consciousness is the Self (ātman). Oṃ, because it cognizes, it is the cognizer (cetana); it is independent in all acts of knowledge and action.
Its state is consciousness, which is said to be the perfect sovereignty consisting of the union of all powers of knowledge and action;
this very [consciousness] is the Self, and not again the body, vital breath, or intellect.
The void, wind, and those accepted by the worldly and others.
Furthermore: this consciousness which has been described is the very nature of the Self, [the source] of the world consisting of existence and non-existence.

As it has been said in the venerable *Ucchuṣmabhairava*: "O Dear One, as long as one does not know 'Who am I?', how can there be objects of knowledge? The means of knowing and the object of knowledge are one; there is no such thing as impurity."

Thus [ends the section]. Knowledge is bondage. Knowledge of objects is bondage; or, by eliding the vowel 'a', ignorance (*ajñāna*) is bondage. They maintain that impurity (*mala*) is ignorance, which is the cause of saṃsāra.
In the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*, it is stated: "The group of matrices (*yoni*) is the cause of the sprout [of the universe]; the body is the *kalā*;
and the expansion of *māyā* as well as the impurity of the self (*ātma-mala*) are also [causes]. (Page 1b) || 2 ||

Bondage consists of the functions of the *kalās*, which is limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*). The support of knowledge is the *Mātṛkā*. (3) There is no cognition whose form is the *Mātṛkā* consisting of the letters from *A* to *KṢa*.

Without the accompaniment of the word "keya," all cognition would not be understood as permeated by the word; for if the eternal form of speech were to depart from consciousness, [it would cease to be knowledge].

For that light shines as reflective awareness precisely because it is grounded in the subject; indeed, due to its being devoid of any internal synthesis of distinctions, it does not remain unperceived for even a moment.
The knowledges that have turned away from external objects are indeed states of rest;
Bhairava is the exertion (*udyama*), the consciousness consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the exertion whose nature is the manifestation of ever-new forms. Bhairava...
[Page 2a] It is the cause for the manifestation of one's own essential nature (*ātmasvasvarūpa*).

In the stabilization of the wheel of power (*śakticakra*), there is the withdrawal of the universe (*viśvasaṃhāra*). As for the "wheel of power," it is that [power] by which the entire world is [constituted]. Of that...

When there is internal reflective awareness (*antarvimarśana*) through continuous connection (*anusandhāna*), there occurs the withdrawal of the universe and its reduction to the fire of supreme consciousness; thus, within the distinctions of waking,
dreaming, and deep sleep, the manifestation of the enjoyment of the Fourth State (*turyābhoga*) arises.
The manifestation of one’s own self as the fourth state (*turya*)— which consists of the radiance of the Self appearing as distinctness within these various forms— is the wonder of its expansion;
this arises eternally for one who is joined with the yoga previously described.
7. Knowledge [arising] during the waking state (*jāgrat*) is that which has as its object things common to all, produced by the external sense organs.
8. Dream is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). 9. Non-discrimination is *māyā*.
Deep sleep is the absence of discernment, non-manifestation; this state of deep sleep consists of *māyā* and is composed of delusion.

The Lord of Heroes (Vīreśa) is the enjoyer of the triad [of states]. (10) He is the one who, through his sovereignty, brings about the wonder of the three states beginning with waking. (11) The stages of yoga are the manifestation of the attainment of identity with the Supreme Reality.
These indicate the repose of the *ropoha* [the state beyond duality].
The power of will (*icchā-śakti*), Umā-Kumārī, the Yoginī, the power of will, is indeed the supreme, transcendent power of the Lord, whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

Śakti is the maiden intent on the play of the creation and destruction of the universe. Whatever is visible— whether the external or internal body— all that which is visible is "I" and "this" belonging to her.

For one whose self consists of the intellect, vital breath, and the body of blue [darkness], there can be no perception of this sleep— which is of the nature of the absence of such [objects] and is void—
as being like one's own limbs according to reality.
Through the investigation of the pure reality, the power of the bound soul [is realized]. ||15||
When one contemplates the entire universe within this reality known as Paramaśiva,
thinking "this is indeed identical with Him," then that [reality] is one whose binding power called *paśutva* (the state of being a bound soul) no longer exists.
Upon seeing this, he becomes a lord of the world, like Sadāśiva.

The knowledge of the Self through *vitarka* is the thought "I am indeed the Self of the universe"; that very same [knowledge] is the *vicāra*. The bliss of the worlds is the bliss of *samādhi*. 17. The worlds... [lo].
The group of perceivers (*grāhakavarga*) flashes forth as it is asked, "What object is perceived?

and it is called "the world" (*loka*) because it is perceived when resting in the state of the subject (*pramātṛpada*); thus, it consists of the letter *ma*, which signifies bliss (*ānanda*). This very [bliss] is its [nature].

The bliss of samādhi. Regarding the generation of the body during the stabilization of power (śaktisandhāna): the previously mentioned power of will (icchāśakti), through identification with that [power] and by its influence, [produces the body] according to one's desire.
His body arises from the conjunction of the elements, the separation of the elements, and the assembly of the universe;
the elements [serve] in the nourishment of the body, the vital breaths, and so forth. (Folio 3b)
Nourishment and maintenance; separation from illness and so forth, meaning the dissociation of the body and other such things from that [source];
and remoteness in terms of place, time, and so on.
Furthermore, when there is the conjunction of the entire universe as the object of knowledge,
its state of being an effect arises upon the application of the previously mentioned powers. From the emergence of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā) comes the sovereignty over the wheels (cakreśatva).

Siddhi 20: When, through the desire for the manifestation of the universal self, he concentrates his power (*śakti*), then, by the dawning of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), the realization "I alone am everything" arises, and his sovereignty (*māheśvarya*)—the state of being the lord of the wheel of his own powers which constitute the universal self—is accomplished. [This occurs] through the pursuit of the great lake...
From that contemplation comes the experience of the potency of the mantra.

[Verse 21] The "Great Lake" (mahāhrada) is that which vomits forth the entire universe— beginning with the supreme consciousness (parā-saṃvit), the will-power (icchā-śakti), and so on, down to the gross objects of knowledge— and which, by virtue of possessing qualities such as being the initiator of the flow of the entire wheel of the sky-farers (khecarī-cakra) and others, transparency, non-obstruction, and profundity, is the object of that contemplation.
By means of the incessant inward-turning contemplation of identity with that [Reality],
there arises the Great Mantra, which consists of the contemplation of the pure "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃtā) and constitutes the vitality (*vīrya*) of all mantras.
Experience is the manifestation [of consciousness] as one's own essential nature.
Thus ends the first unfolding, titled "The Revelation of the Extraction of Mantras," from the *Śāmbhavopāyaprakāśa*. 1.

The mantra is the mind; the mantra is the very mind of the worshipper who has attained identity with it through being intent on the contemplation of the deity of the mantra. 1. The practitioner is effort. 2. Uncreated...

What effort is required? One who serves as the practitioner bestows identity with the deity of the mantra. The secret of the mantra is the existence of the body of knowledge (vidyā-śarīra). [The body of knowledge...]

The secret and the innermost essence (*upaniṣad*) of these mantras is the flashing forth of the self-awareness of the perfect "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃvimarśa*), which consists of the non-difference from the entire universe remaining as pure existence within this mass of sounds, and which resides in the womb of the consciousness.
Expansion is the dream of undifferentiated knowledge. (p.
4b) It is the expansion of the mind within the manifold of mantra-attainments in the womb; it is satisfaction with that alone, while [ordinary] knowledge is common to all people.
The state of dream is impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*) whose nature is limited subjectivity;
it is rooted in duality, characterized by the absence of consciousness, consisting of conceptual construction, and is an error.
As it is stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra], regarding those [dreams] during meditative absorption (*samādhi*): [text continues].
It is established that there is no emergence from old age. In the natural arising of Vidyā, Khecarī is the state of Śiva;
it is the supreme non-dual manifestation, the nature of pure Vidyā.

She who moves in the sky of primordial awakening is revealed as Khecarī; the Guru is the means. 6. Therefore, here, in the attainment of the potency of the mudrā and mantra, [resides] the wheel of the Mātṛkās.

The awakening of the disciple occurs—this is the ellipsis. It consists of the complete immersion in one’s own essential nature, which is a mass of consciousness-bliss, brought about by the manifestation of the will for supreme bliss (*anuttarānanda*) through the revelation of the reality of the *unmeṣa* (the unfolding) of the *īśana* (the power of the Lord). It is perfect.

It becomes excellent; therefore, from the grace of the Guru, it belongs to the disciple—this is the remainder [of the sense]. For the body is the bird that has been consecrated by all as the subject (pramātṛ).
The body, consisting of gross, subtle, and other forms, is the oblation being offered into the supreme fire of consciousness by that great yogi.

Knowledge is food (8). That which was previously called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the "food" (*anna*) of yogins because it is being consumed; furthermore, [it is so called] because of the reflective awareness of its own nature.

That food of his, being of such a nature, causes complete satisfaction and is the cause for resting in one's own self. Upon the emergence of knowledge, there is the vision of that object as a dream. 9.
Through immersion into Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), the emergence of the manifold proliferation of thought-constructs (vikalpaprapañca),
which consists of duality, clearly occurs; this is the second [stage], the illumination of the Empowered Means (śāktopāya).
The Third Unfolding: The Self is the mind;
that which is permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects is the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and other functions such as conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
(p. 5b) Nor is the mind formless; rather, by taking recourse to the functions of *sattva* and so forth, it wanders through various wombs (*yoni*).

This is the meaning of [the term] *ātman* or *aṇu*. Knowledge is bondage. That knowledge which consists of the functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth—composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion—and which takes the form of the manifestation of its appropriate distinctions, is bondage. It is precisely because he is bound by that [knowledge] that he transmigrates. As it has been said in the venerable *Tantrasadbhāva*:
Established in *sattva*, established in *rajas*, and experiencing the qualities of *tamas*—
thus does the embodied soul wander, going from one state to another. [End of section on] *kalā* and the rest.

The non-discrimination of the principles (tattva) refers to [the state] of the principles beginning with *kalā*— which take the form of agency and so forth, such as the power of illusion (*māyā*)— and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*),
along with the sheaths (*kañcuka*), the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the gross body.
The non-discrimination of things that exist as distinct—
which consists in the apprehension of those very things regarded as separate as having a non-separate nature— is what is called the reality of sameness (sāmānya-tattva).
The manifold world is a mere illusion; it is the withdrawal of the *kalās* from the body— whether that body be gross, subtle, or supreme—
from the various elemental portions (*tattva-bhāga*) of the *kalās*, such as earth and so forth.

The remaining portion [of the instruction] is that the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the principles from Vyāpti down to the end must be practiced through the meditation on their dissolution into their own respective causes;
this occurs precisely through the mastery of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the elements (*bhūta*).
The dissolution of the various elements within the central channel among the channels that carry the vital breaths and other flows;
and the victory over the elements, which is the bringing about of their absorption.

The isolation of the elements, the withdrawal of the mind from them, the distinctness of the elements, and the state of being a pure, independent conscious self uncolored by them— these belong to the yogi.

The remainder is that they are not to be cultivated. Success comes from the veil of delusion; that is, success is attained through the sequence of dhāraṇā and so forth as previously described, [arising] from the obscuration caused by delusion.

Through the enjoyment of reality, there is victory over innate knowledge; through the conquest and overcoming of delusion (*moha*) and illusion (*māyā*), what kind [of state] is it? It is that which culminates in the pacification of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), reaching the infinite.
From that which possesses such expansion and breadth, there arises the attainment of victory over innate knowledge (sahajavidyā).
[Verse 6] The second hand is the waking state; it is the pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) of the waking state.

The second [aspect], which is the object of awareness consisting of the manifestation of the knowable (*vedyābhāsa*), is that which is to be contemplated as "this" (*idantā*) in relation to the self-sense of "I" (*ahantā*) that consists of perfect reflective awareness (*pūrṇavimarśa*). It is vigilant regarding the pervasive power of poetic wisdom (*kāvya-āpti-ojas*).
The meaning is that he whose rays constitute the body of the universe is such that the entire world shines forth as if it were his own radiance. 8. [Regarding] the dancer—

The Self dances within, its own true nature concealed, producing through the play of its own vibration the manifold expansion of various stages such as waking and so forth, which have the support [of the body] as their root.
Manifesting the division of the self, he is the dancer; the stage is the inner self, the stage being the place for assuming various roles,
and the inner self is the witness.

(p. 7a) There exists a certain manifestation whose essence is either predominantly void or predominantly vital breath, constrained by the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*); therein this *jīva* has established its seat and, through the sequence of the activity of its own organs, manifests the drama of the world. The senses are the spectators for the revelation of this drama of transmigratory existence.
They directly realize their own nature, filled with supreme joy, through inward-turnedness; by the power of the intellect,
there is the attainment of the true essence, for the intellect is the discernment of one's own real nature.
And in drama as well, through the power of the spectator’s refined aesthetic sensibility, there occurs the manifestation of the subtle internal vibration of the being whose nature is radiance.
Success in sattvic expression is obtained through skill of intellect and other means. "Siddha" means the state of independence;
"siddha" means perfected, the state of independence, which is innate knowledge and agency.
The sovereignty that consists of reality and so forth, which brings the entire universe under its control;
just as it is there,
so it is elsewhere wherever the yogi manifests himself within a body.

pṛ0 7ba) Manifestation occurs there in whatever manner it may; elsewhere, it arises for one who is always attentive to everything. (14) The depositing of the seed: within the seed, which is of the nature of the supreme power (*paraśakti*).
The ellipsis is that one must repeatedly apply attention—that is, fix the mind—upon the Cause of the Universe.
15. Seated upon his seat, he sinks into the lake of bliss.
That in which one remains eternally through absolute oneness is the "seat" (āsana); he who stands there possesses the supreme Śākta power,
having abandoned both higher and lower meditation and concentration (dhyāna-dhāraṇā).
He who, through constant inward-turnedness, reflects upon that very [Self] without the effort of all external activities,
effortlessly sinks into the ocean of supreme nectar, [rendering] the body and so forth [insignificant].
Through contraction, withdrawal, and absorption, one becomes identical with that; one brings about the manifestation of one's own measure—
the measure belonging to one's own consciousness.

The portion of the self whose nature is the congealing of the essence of consciousness (cidrasa), being of that very form, brings about a manifestation consisting of the appearance of the desired object and subject, and displays it as something created. [This occurs] upon the destruction of ignorance (avidyā). 17. Vidya-vināśe.
The destruction of birth occurs when, upon the non-destruction of knowledge, there is a constant manifestation characterized by being ever-emerged [from ignorance]; for birth,
which has karma as its auxiliary cause for the arising of knowledge, is [thereby] destroyed.
The destruction—that is, the dissolution—of the collection consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, has indeed occurred. 18.
In the [letters] beginning with the *ka*-group, [the goddesses] such as Māheśvarī are the *paśus*.

The ellipsis is that they become the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātrī*). It has been stated in general that the "mother" (*mātṛkā*) is the substratum of knowledge; however, this [present case] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even for one who has attained the reality (*tattva*).

The distinction is that [the Lord] causes even those presiding over animal-like people—such as Heṣī and others—to be deluded by means of the repetition of the word "api" (even). Thus ends the nineteenth [verse]. And in the three...

(p. 8b) "It should be poured like oil upon the fourth" means that in all three stages—waking and so forth—the fourth state, which consists of the light of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and whose essence is the nectar of the bliss of the Fourth (*turyānanda*), should be poured like oil. Just as oil, spreading more and more progressively, reaches its substrate, so too should it be poured upon all three stages by means of the flavor of the Fourth, which vibrates at both the initial and final limits and consists of the subsiding of the emergence (*unmeṣa*).
One should pervade even the twelve [centers] through the method of support (*avaṣṭambha-yukti*), by which one attains identification with that [reality].
Immersed, one should enter with one's own mind; immersed, [one should enter] from the body.

Quelling the state of being a limited subject, one should enter into the nature of non-conceptuality. 21. In the practice of the vital breath (prāṇa), there is the vision of equality; [the movement] of the prāṇa is outward.

The meaning is that, by virtue of being of the nature of a mass of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandaghana*), experience becomes uniform in its single form across all states, as it were, through its slow and steady expansion. 22. In the midst... [the best...]

Existence: At the prior and posterior limits, due to the dissolution of the fourth flavor (turya-rasa), in the middle— the intermediate state— one who is inferior or superior becomes entirely contemptible,
consisting of the manifestation of duality.
pṛ0 9a) One is not deluded by the *tuṣas* (husks). 23. Through the continuous connection of one's own internal cognitions regarding the *mātrās*, that which was lost arises again.
When one perceives the measure [of reality] within all objects, contemplating everywhere that "this entire universe is I," as the nature of the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), then,
due to the granting of the boon previously mentioned, [the world-appearance] is destroyed.

The meaning is that for the yogi, there occurs a re-emergence of the nature consisting of the wonder of the fourth state (*turya*); he becomes equal to Śiva through the constant cultivation of the fourth state. 33. *śivatulyo jāyate turyapariśīlanāt*.
Because there is no further excellence [to be attained], he has reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta);
he is equal to the Lord Śiva, who is a mass of pure, autonomous consciousness-bliss; [only] the vine of his body remains.
By its melting away, he becomes equal to that;
the meaning is that he becomes manifest as Śiva himself. The bodily conduct is called a "vow" (vrata) according to the perspective already described, [in which one] is equal to Śiva.
For this yogin who exists with the sense of identity as Śiva (śivāhaṃbhāva), that which constitutes his activity or conduct within the body is itself his vow (vrata)—
that which must be practiced according to rule— and not anything else.
A vow distinct from the maintenance of the body has been prescribed:
35. Recitation of the narrative: "I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, Śiva, the ultimate cause."

When one has ascended to the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the uncreated "I," which consists of the great mantra of the Self— the nature of which is the contemplation of the supreme "I" as both eternal and non-eternal— then whatever discourse or other activity occurs [is of that same nature].

Thus, from the uninterrupted turning of the reflective awareness of one's own self as the deity, the *ajāpa* arises. (36) Giving is the knowledge of the Self; it is called "giving" (*dāna*) because [the Self] is given.

By this, the knowledge of the Self is imparted to the disciples. He who stands as the Lord, the cause of knowledge, within the assembly of the Mothers of the Paśus in the wheels (cakras) beginning with Māheśvarī; 37.
That which exists as the substrate (bhṛti) is the power of knowledge;
it is capable of being taught, and by means of the power of knowledge, it is able to awaken the word to its own power regarding the object. 38. svashakti.

Since this entire universe is an accumulation [of his parts], Śiva is therefore called "Yukta" (the Joined One); thus, according to the perspective of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), he is Śiva because he has joined this entire world according to his power.
Likewise, the universe consists of His own power;
it is the accumulation of His own power, which is the nature of consciousness,
appearing as the expansion of the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
"Stasis and dissolution, outward-facing manifestation, and repose within the conscious subject— this is the accumulation of one's own powers," thus it continues.

Even when those [states] arise, there is no exclusion [of the fourth state], because of the absence of [ordinary] consciousness; for even when the distinctions of creation and so forth emerge, there is no movement from this fourth state of the yogi.
Because [pleasure and pain] are obtained from that which consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) characterized by wonder, there is an external mentalization of pleasure and pain;
for pleasure and pain, born from contact with an object of cognition, possess an "this-ness" (*idantā*) externally, just like blue and other such objects.

The contemplation of the nature of light is pure awareness (*saṃvedana*), and not like the worldly [consciousness] which involves contact with the "I-sense" (*ahaṃtā*); for the yogi is one whose limited subjectivity consisting of the eightfold subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) has been stilled.
How can an existent being be touched by pleasure and pain?
One who is liberated from that is "kevalin"— specifically liberated from those two, namely pleasure and pain.

Even through mere mental construction (*saṃskāra*), he is internally united with that which is solitary, whose nature is that of the pure subject who is consciousness alone; yet, his karma is bound by delusion. 43.

The self (ātman), obstructed by delusion—that is, by ignorance—is described as being a single mass of that [ignorance]; it is perpetually stained by the impressions of both auspicious and inauspicious [actions]. When the sense of duality is set aside, there is the state of performing actions for other creations; [this refers to] the body, vital breath, and so forth.
When the distinction between the Self and the ego-sense (*abhimāna*) is set aside (p. 11a),
and once [the ego] has been cast away through the emergence of the nature of pure consciousness (*cidghana*),
its status as the object of another creation occurs exactly as desired.

The state of being the creator of created objects arises from its own inherent power of instrumentality (karaṇa-śakti), as established through direct experience; and this is not impossible for it, because it possesses the power of instrumentality.
From its own experience itself— in such states as volition and dreaming— the power of the instrument, which is the Self’s capacity to construct various specific objects, is indeed established. 45.

The vitalization of the three feet and so forth refers to the state of being oriented toward the three— creation, maintenance, and dissolution— as designated by the word "existence," as well as the state of attachment and inward-turning toward them.
Among the various states, that which is the foremost,
consisting of a mass of bliss, known as the Fourth (turya), though veiled by the power of māyā,
[remains] during the intervals between the enjoyment of various objects and so forth.
One should effect the attainment of that Self which appears like lightning amidst the clouds; this is like the stability of the mind within the body, the senses, and external objects. 46.
Even when there is an outward orientation consisting of the appearance of external objects and the involuntary functioning of the body, within a state of mental abiding that is inward-turned,
one is nevertheless sustained by that fourth state.
One should not make a mark [of pride]. 47. Because of desire, there is an outward departure;
he who is carried away from the womb is led to another womb, and thus he is called *saṃvāhya*.
*Saṃvāhya* means one who is led (*nīyate*) from one womb to another. *Ka*... [end of fragment]

The bound soul (paśu), whose nature is [limited] selfhood, due to the desire for that [Self], proceeds outward toward objects because of the cause known as the impurity of finitude (āṇavamala), which consists of the sense of being incomplete.

You alone exist; there is never any absorption in an inward-turned nature. Then, through the dissolution of that cognition which has ascended [to the higher state], there is the dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*).
"That" refers to the cognition intent on the discernment of that [Reality] which has ascended to the fourth state (*turya-pada*).
For that yogi who possesses such consciousness,

there occurs the destruction— that is, the pacification— of the state of being a limited subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), which belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) that is carried along by desire; [this results in] pure consciousness alone.

The meaning is that [the Self] shines forth precisely by means of its state of being "made of thirst" (tṛmayatā). 49. He who is not yet liberated from the sheath of the elements (bhūtakañcukī) is, for the most part, equal to the Lord (pati). 50. "At that time"—meaning, when desire has ceased and the individual soul (jīva) has been dissolved, and when the conceit of being a subject consisting of the sixfold person (ṣaṭka-pramātṛtā) has fallen away—he becomes one whose elements form a sheath like a body, such that the elements are like a covering distinct from him, as if they were a garment, and do not touch the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā); being thus liberated, he is destined for Nirvāṇa and is, for the most part (bhūyas), equal to the Lord.

One who has entered the supreme nature of the Lord, which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), is another, full [being]; according to the principle of the stated Sūtra, "the vow is the functioning within the body," even while situated in a body that is like a blade of grass, he is untouched by the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of subjectivity. (This is the moment of cessation. Why does the natural connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) not cease for him at that very moment, even though he is [free from] the sheath of the elements (*bhūtakañcuka*)? 51. Thus [he asks].

The innate connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is "innate" (*naisargika*) because it has come forth from the very nature of the Self, which is characterized by freedom; for consciousness is indeed the Blessed Lady.

Desiring to manifest the manifold variety of the universe, [the Supreme Lord], preceded by the manifestation of contraction, assumes the stage of the grasper— which consists of the vitalizing breath (*prāṇa*) that is the radiance of the entire contracted universe—
and [thereby brings about] the appearance of the world as the object of perception.
Because it vibrates with the self, this natural bond with the vital breath (prāṇa), first manifested through her own sovereignty, [arises] from the restraint within the middle of the nose.
51. [From] the restraint within the middle of the nose...
In the right, left, and suṣumnā channels—
which are the primary forms of the entire network of channels—
[the breath flows] through the right, left, and suṣumnā.
Because it flows crookedly through the positions of the dhyāna-nāḍīs and the nostrils,
the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) is called Kuṭilavāhinī; within that [is the following].

Within that, there is the intermediate consciousness; and within that, the primary [consciousness] is that whose nature consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because it is the innermost of all.
By means of *saṃyama* upon that, there arises internal perception.
What more need be said here? For this is the supreme samādhi, shining forth from all scriptures and free from emergence (nirvyutthāna).
The universe, which has arisen from the essential nature of the conscious Self (caitanya-ātman),
returns again and again— through the dissolution of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of duality and by way of manifoldness— to its original state.

And "closing" (mīlana) is the closing [of the senses] toward consciousness; furthermore, for the yogi who is intent upon supreme yoga, it takes the form of the unfolding of the essential nature of the self as consciousness— this is the individual means (āṇava).
The third unfolding, the manifestation of the organ of excretion, is concluded.
This commentary on the Śivasūtras is finished.
This has been purified by the illustrious Śrī Sāhibakaula Śivanātha for the sake of the great king Rāmasiṃha.
